name: Artemis
title: Greek goddess worshipped in Ephesus
summary: In the ancient city of Ephesus, Artemis – known as Diana in Roman context – held a central place as a goddess of fertility and motherhood with deep roots in Anatolian religious tradition. Although she is not a biblical figure, the cult of Artemis plays an important role in the narrative of Acts chapter 19. When the apostle Paul preached the gospel in Ephesus over a long period, many began to turn away from idol worship. This triggered strong reactions from the silversmith Demetrius and other craftsmen who made their living by producing cult objects connected to the temple of Artemis – regarded as one of the seven wonders of antiquity. The subsequent riots clearly show how the spread of Christian faith challenged not only religious, but also economic and social power structures in the ancient world.

keyEvents.title: Paul's preaching in Ephesus
keyEvents.description: Paul worked in Ephesus for over two years and preached the gospel, first in the synagogue and then in the school of Tyrannus, so that many in the province of Asia heard the Lord's word.

keyEvents.title: Burning of magic books in Ephesus
keyEvents.description: Many who had practiced sorcery gathered their books and burned them publicly. This testified to the deep impact the gospel had in Artemis' home city.

keyEvents.title: Demetrius stirred up a riot
keyEvents.description: The silversmith Demetrius, who made silver shrines of Artemis, gathered the craftsmen and incited them against Paul because his preaching threatened both their livelihood and the cult of Artemis.

keyEvents.title: Riots in Ephesus
keyEvents.description: The crowd became furious and shouted for about two hours: "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!" The city was filled with confusion, and two of Paul's traveling companions were dragged into the theater.

keyEvents.title: The city clerk calmed the crowd
keyEvents.description: The city clerk in Ephesus finally intervened, reminded the crowd that the cult of Artemis was not under threat, and urged them to resolve the matter legally rather than through rebellion.

versions.summary: Artemis (also known as Diana) was not a biblical figure but a Greek goddess worshipped in Ephesus. She is mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles in connection with the riots in Ephesus, where the silversmith Demetrius and other craftsmen protested against the apostle Paul's preaching because it threatened the cult surrounding the Temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

footnotes.text: The Temple of Artemis in Ephesus (Artemision) was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. It was originally built around 550 BC under the direction of the Cretan architect Chersiphron. The temple was destroyed and rebuilt several times, including after the arson committed by Herostratus in 356 BC. The ruins were rediscovered by archaeologist John Turtle Wood in 1869.

The Ephesian Artemis was significantly different from the classical Greek huntress goddess Artemis. The Ephesian version was primarily a fertility and mother goddess with roots in Anatolian religion, likely connected to the older goddess Cybele. Her cult image was decorated with what has traditionally been interpreted as many breasts, but which some scholars believe may represent bull testicles or other fertility symbols.

The Greek word Ἄρτεμις (Artemis) appears in the New Testament exclusively in Acts 19. The Latin equivalent is Diana. Demetrius's silver shrines (ναούς ἀργυροῦς) were likely miniature models of the Temple of Artemis or of the goddess's sanctuary, sold as religious souvenirs to pilgrims visiting Ephesus.

The riots in Ephesus illustrate the economic dimension of idolatry in the ancient world. Demetrius's protest was not only motivated by religion but stemmed from fear of losing income from the production and sale of cult objects. This provides important insight into the socio-economic challenges the early church faced when the gospel challenged established religious and commercial structures.

The theater in Ephesus, where the riots took place (Acts 19:29), was a massive amphitheater with seating for approximately 25,000 spectators. It is today one of the best-preserved ruins in Ephesus and has been thoroughly excavated by Austrian archaeologists since the early 1900s.

The city clerk (Greek: γραμματεύς) in Ephesus was a high-ranking official responsible for the city's official documents and correspondence with Roman authorities. His intervention during the riots (Acts 19:35–41) shows that he feared Roman reprisals if the unrest was not stopped, since unauthorized public gatherings could be considered rebellion by the Roman provincial authorities.
